passages.t: Not a short arm, but a wall of sin
passages.happening:
‘Surely the arm of the LORD is not too short to save, nor His ear too dull to hear’ (verse 1). ‘But your iniquities have built barriers between you and your God, and your sins have hidden His face from you, so that He does not hear’ (verse 2).

The prophet names what has built the wall. Their hands are stained with blood, their lips speak lies, their tongues mutter injustice (verse 3). No one calls for justice or pleads a case honestly (verse 4). ‘They hatch the eggs of vipers and weave a spider’s web’ (verse 5). Their webs cannot be made into clothing (verse 6). ‘Their feet run to evil; they are swift to shed innocent blood’ (verse 7). ‘The way of peace they have not known, and there is no justice in their tracks’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 58 answered the complaint that God did not notice the people's fasting. Chapter 59 answers a deeper complaint, that God seems unable or unwilling to save. The answer echoes 50:2: his hand is not too short. The problem is sin.

The chapter describes a community in moral collapse: bloodshed, lies, crooked courts, and people who turn from evil becoming prey. Most scholars place it after the return, when the hopes of the return had not come true and Judah was small, poor and under Persian rule. Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi speak to similar disappointment and similar sins. On the traditional reading, the same charges fit Judah before the exile, which Isaiah and Micah condemned.

The pictures come from nature. Viper eggs bring death when hatched. A spider's web looks like cloth but cannot be woven into a garment. Their schemes are either deadly or useless. The list moves through the body, hands, fingers, lips, tongue and feet, all turned to harm.
passages.later: Paul quotes verses 7 and 8 in his case that all have sinned, Jew and Gentile alike: ‘Their feet are swift to shed blood’ (Romans 3:15). Micah had brought the same charge against Jerusalem's leaders in his own day (Micah 3).
passages.asks: The people thought God could not save them, and the prophet says their sins had hidden his face. Ask whether anything in your life has built a wall between you and God. And ask whether you are quicker to doubt God's arm than to look at your own hands.

passages.t: The confession: groping like the blind at noon
passages.happening:
Now the people speak, and they confess. ‘Therefore justice is far from us, and righteousness does not reach us’ (verse 9). They hope for light and find darkness. ‘Like the blind, we feel our way along the wall, groping like those without eyes’ (verse 10). ‘We stumble at midday as in the twilight’ (verse 10). They growl like bears and moan like doves, hoping for justice and finding none (verse 11).

‘For our transgressions are multiplied before You, and our sins testify against us’ (verse 12). They know their sins: rebelling against the LORD, turning away from God, speaking oppression and lies (verse 13).

‘So justice is turned away, and righteousness stands at a distance. For truth has stumbled in the public square, and honesty cannot enter’ (verse 14). Truth is missing, and whoever turns from evil becomes prey (verse 15). ‘The LORD looked and was displeased that there was no justice’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The voice changes. The prophet spoke of you and they. Now the people speak of themselves and admit that the charges are true. Prayers from the time after the exile, in Ezra 9, Nehemiah 9 and Daniel 9, have the same shape: leaders confess the sins of the whole people, their own generation included.

The public square was a town's open plaza, often beside the city gate, where the elders sat to hear lawsuits and settle disputes. When truth stumbles there, the whole system of justice fails, and ordinary people have nowhere to turn.

The word justice, mishpat, appears five times in the chapter, and every time it is missing. The right ordering of life together has broken down, and the people say so.
passages.later: Ezra prays the same kind of confession for the returned community: ‘Our iniquities are higher than our heads’ (Ezra 9:6). Daniel confesses for his whole people, ‘we have sinned and done wrong’ (Daniel 9:5).
passages.asks: The people stop blaming God and confess their own part. Ask what it would sound like for your church or community to pray verse 12 honestly. And ask where truth has stumbled in the places where you have a voice.

passages.t: The LORD puts on righteousness, and the Redeemer comes to Zion
passages.happening:
‘He saw that there was no man; He was amazed that there was no one to intercede’ (verse 16). ‘So His own arm brought salvation, and His own righteousness sustained Him’ (verse 16).

‘He put on righteousness like a breastplate, and the helmet of salvation on His head’ (verse 17). He put on garments of vengeance and wrapped himself in zeal. He will repay according to their deeds, fury to his enemies, even to the islands (verse 18). From west to east they will fear the name of the LORD, for he will come like a raging flood (verse 19).

The LORD declares that the Redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from transgression (verse 20). And his covenant with them is this: his Spirit will not depart from them, nor his words from their mouths, or the mouths of their children and grandchildren, from now on and forever (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
No one is able to set things right, so God acts himself. The word for intercede in verse 16 is the word used of the Servant in 53:12, who made intercession for the transgressors. The missing intercessor of this chapter is the one chapter 53 described.

The armor is a soldier's: breastplate, helmet and cloak. Pictures of gods as warriors were common in the ancient world, and Israel sang that the LORD is a warrior. What stands out is what he wears: righteousness, salvation, vengeance and zeal, qualities and not metal.

The Redeemer, the go'el, was the nearest relative who bought back family land or a relative sold into slavery. God comes as the nearest relative of a helpless people. He comes to those who turn from transgression, so the line runs between those who turn and those who do not, not between peoples.

Verse 21 ends with a covenant of Spirit and word that recalls 51:16 and looks ahead to 61:1.
passages.later: Paul quotes verses 20 and 21 in their Greek form to say that God's covenant with Israel still stands: “The Deliverer will come from Zion; He will remove godlessness from Jacob” (Romans 11:26). The armor becomes the believer's: ‘the breastplate of righteousness arrayed’ (Ephesians 6:14).
passages.hard:
God puts on garments of vengeance and repays fury to his enemies. How does that fit with his love?

Some readers find this at odds with the God of compassion elsewhere in Isaiah. Vengeance in the Bible is not personal spite but the restoring of justice by the rightful judge, and it belongs to God so that people will not take it into their own hands (Romans 12:19). The setting is a world where the innocent are prey and there is no justice. A God who never acted against oppressors would not be loving to their victims. And the same passage offers redemption to anyone who turns from transgression (verse 20), so the line between enemies and redeemed is moral, not ethnic.

Readers still differ on how to hold wrath and love together, but Scripture holds both. Nothing here gives anyone a warrant to carry out God's vengeance on another person.
passages.asks: God looked, saw no one to step in, and acted himself. Ask where you have waited for someone else to step in when God was asking you to pray. And ask what it means for you that the Redeemer comes to those who turn.
